human-impacts-ecosystems-s1.title: Stream insects above and below a mine drainage pipe

table.caption: Insect larvae counted in one kick-net sample at four sites on a stream (invented data for practice)

human-impacts-ecosystems-s2.title: Coral cover and summer water temperature on a reef

plot.label: Dual-axis line graph from 2010 to 2022: live coral cover on a reef falls from 45 to 18 percent, dropping most in 2016 and 2020, while peak summer water temperature rises from 29.0 to 30.6 degrees Celsius with spikes in 2016 and 2020; invented data

items.q: How does the number of mayfly and stonefly larvae change downstream of the pipe?
options: They rise just below the pipe, then fall farther down
They crash below the pipe, then recover
They stay about the same from site to site
They fall at each site and do not recover

why.correct: They drop from 48 upstream to 2 just below the pipe, then recover to 15 at 2 km and 40 at 6 km as the water improves.
options: They fall just below the pipe, from 48 to 2.
Right: 48, then 2, then 15, then 40.
They range from 2 to 48.
They recover to 40 at 6 km.

items.q: Why are mayflies and stoneflies useful as indicator species here?
options: They need clean water, so they track its quality
They thrive in polluted water, so they show where pollution is
They eat the pollutants, so they clean the stream
They are the largest insects, so they are easy to count

why.correct: They need clean, oxygen-rich water, so their numbers rise and fall with water quality. Their crash at site 2 signals pollution; midges and worms, which tolerate low oxygen, increase there.
options: Right: their numbers follow dissolved oxygen closely.
They do the opposite; tolerant midges and worms thrive there.
They do not clean the stream; their numbers just reflect its quality.
Size is not what makes an indicator species useful.

items.q: Find the percent change in mayfly and stonefly larvae from site 1 to site 2.

mistakes.why: You divided by the site 2 count. Divide by the starting (site 1) count, 48.
The count fell, so the change is negative: about -95.8%.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data best support?
options: The discharge improves water quality for the insects
Midges and worms cause the oxygen to drop
Water quality is worst 6 km below the pipe
The discharge harms water quality near the pipe

why.correct: Below the pipe, dissolved oxygen and sensitive insects both fall while tolerant insects rise, and all recover downstream, so the discharge is lowering water quality near the pipe.
options: Sensitive insects crash below the pipe.
The drop starts at the pipe; tolerant insects respond to it.
Site 4 is nearly back to upstream levels.
Right: oxygen and sensitive insects drop at site 2 and recover by site 4.

items.q: What happens to live coral cover in the years with the highest summer temperatures?
options: It rises in the hottest years
It drops the most in the coolest years
It drops sharply in the hottest years
It stays the same whatever the temperature

why.correct: In 2016 and 2020, the two hottest summers, coral cover drops sharply (42 to 28, and 27 to 19 percent). In cooler years it changes little.
options: Cover falls, not rises, in 2016 and 2020.
The coolest years show the smallest changes.
Right: the biggest drops come in 2016 and 2020.
It falls from 45 to 18 percent.

items.q: Which process explains the link between hot summers and coral loss?
options: Warm water dissolves the coral skeleton directly
Heat makes corals expel the algae that feed them
Hot water brings more algae, which smother the coral
Warm water carries more oxygen, which poisons coral

why.correct: Heat stress makes corals expel the algae that live in their tissues and feed them by photosynthesis. The corals turn white (bleach), and if the heat lasts they starve and die.
options: The main effect of heat is losing the algae, not dissolving the skeleton.
Right: that is coral bleaching.
Bleaching is the loss of the algae living inside the coral.
Warm water holds less oxygen, not more.

items.q: Find the percent change in live coral cover from 2010 to 2022.

mistakes.why: -27 is the change in percentage points (45 to 18). Percent change divides by the old value: -27 / 45 × 100 = -60%.
You divided by the 2022 value. Divide by the old (2010) value, 45.

options: A species whose numbers reveal the health of its environment
A species that has more effect on its community than its numbers suggest
The first species to colonize bare rock
A species that eats a wide range of foods

why.correct: An indicator species is one whose presence, absence or health reveals the condition of its environment, such as mayfly larvae for clean, oxygen-rich streams.
options: Right: its presence or absence signals conditions.
That describes a keystone species.
That describes a pioneer species.
That describes a generalist species.

items.q: Coral reefs are also harmed by sediment from coastal construction and farms. How does sediment harm them?
options: It raises the water temperature to bleaching levels
It adds oxygen that the coral is unable to use
It makes the water too fresh for coral
It blocks light from the coral's algae

why.correct: Sediment clouds the water, blocking the sunlight the coral's algae need for photosynthesis, and it can settle on and smother the coral.
options: Sediment does not cause bleaching heat.
Sediment does not add oxygen.
Sediment does not lower salinity.
Right: less light means less food for the coral.

items.q: How does an oil spill harm seabirds?
options: Oil warms the water so fish move away from the birds
Oil makes the water more acidic, dissolving eggshells
Oil mats feathers and poisons birds that preen
Oil adds nutrients that cause algae to cover the birds

why.correct: Oil coats feathers so they mat together and lose their waterproofing and insulation; birds become cold and cannot float or fly, and they swallow oil while preening.
options: The main harm is to the birds' feathers and bodies.
Oil does not acidify water in this way.
Right: both hypothermia and poisoning.
Oil is not a nutrient that feeds algae.

items.q: Where do most microplastics in the ocean come from?
options: Natural rock weathered into tiny plastic grains
Larger plastic broken up by sun and waves
Plankton that build plastic shells
Oil spills that harden into beads on the seafloor

why.correct: Most microplastics are pieces of larger plastic broken down by sunlight and waves, plus fibers shed from synthetic clothing and small beads from some products.
options: Plastic is made by people; rocks do not weather into plastic.
Right: big plastic becomes many small pieces.
No plankton make plastic.
Spilled oil does not turn into plastic beads.

items.q: Why are microplastics a problem for ocean food webs?
options: Animals eat them, and they carry toxins
They release oxygen that bleaches coral
They warm the water by absorbing sunlight
They break down quickly into nutrients for algae

why.correct: Small animals mistake them for food, which fills their guts without nourishing them, and plastics can carry toxic chemicals that move up the food chain.
options: Right: they block feeding and carry toxins up food chains.
Plastics do not release oxygen.
Their main harm is being eaten, not warming.
Plastics last a very long time and are not nutrients.

items.q: Which response is best fitted to cleaning up oil that has spilled into a calm harbor?
options: Adding fertilizer so algae grow over the oil
Draining the harbor into the open sea
Adding limestone to neutralize the oil
Booms to hold the oil and skimmers to lift it

why.correct: Floating booms contain the slick so skimmers can collect it from the surface. This fits a calm, enclosed harbor.
options: Fertilizer would feed a mass of algae; it would not remove the oil.
That spreads the oil; it does not remove it.
Limestone neutralizes acid; oil is not an acid.
Right: booms hold the slick so it can be skimmed off.

items.q: A coastal town's beaches and reef are covered in plastic litter washed out from the town's storm drains. Propose a town-level solution and explain how it works.

why.correct: The solution fits the scale (a town) and the source (storm drains), and it says how it works: screens catch litter before it reaches the sea.

specific.frame: The town could ___, which reduces ocean plastic because ___.

action.label: Solution
options: fit screens on storm drains and ban single-use plastic bags
ask other countries to stop making plastic
add more fish to the reef

why.1: That is outside a town's power and not fitted to its storm drains.
why.2: More fish do not reduce the plastic.

how.label: How it works
options: litter is caught before it reaches the sea, and less is made in the first place
plastic dissolves faster in drain water
fish eat the plastic and remove it

why.1: Plastic does not dissolve in water.
why.2: Fish eating plastic harms them; it is the problem, not the fix.

specific.model: The town could fit screens on storm drains and ban single-use plastic bags, which reduces ocean plastic because litter is caught before it reaches the sea and less plastic is used in the first place.

items.q: A beach cleanup collects 1,250 pieces of plastic along 500 meters of shoreline. Write the setup for the pieces per meter, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Pieces per meter puts pieces on top: 1,250 / 500.
That is meters per piece. Pieces per meter is 1,250 / 500 = 2.5.
